2. The said proceeding is in complaint Case No 892a of 1991 in the court of a Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka; it was started on a complaint filed by the appellant on 14 January 1991 against the accused respondents under section 408 and 420 of the Penal Code. The appellant is the Chief Executive of two Industrial establishments and the respondents are the officers in charge of the finance and accounts section of the appellant's establishments. Allegation as stated in the complaint petition is that the accused persons, by practicising deception and also by forging some cheques and vouchers, misappropriated an amount of Tk.1.25 crore and some odd in the period from 1987 to 1990. The Magistrate took cognigance thereon and the accused having appeared before him charges under two heads were framed on 1 October 1991 and two witnesses for the prosecution were also examined by 13 January, 1992. The accused respondents filed an application before the High Court Division under section 561A Cr. P.C. for quashing the proceeding but withdrew it when no rule was issued thereon. They then filed a revisional application under section 438 Cr. P.C. before the Sessions Judge challenging the framing of the charges, but it was rejected by an order dated 10 October, 1992.They then filed a Civil Suit-Title Suit No 171 of 1992-on 13. 8 .92 against the complainant- appellant and his Establishments for declaration of title and recovery of compensation to the extent of Tk. 1.27 Thereafter they filed an application on 14 November, 1992 before the trial Court under section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code for staying further proceedings of the criminal case till disposal of their suit, but the application was rejected by an order dated 21 November 1992. Thereupon one of the accused-appellants filed a revisional application under section 439 of the Code before the High Court Division challenging the trial Court's order refusing stay of the proceedings. This application was allowed and the rule issued thereon was made absolute by the impugned order of the High Court Division. By this order, the proceeding of criminal case was stayed for a period of six months. This period is going to expire on 8 September, 1994. 

 3. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Counsel for the appellant has pointed out that as the period of stay is going to expire very soon the appeal has become practically infructuous. The impugned order of the High Court Division shows that though it expressed doubt about the justification for staying the criminal proceeding it granted the stay for a limited period on the assumption that the civil suit might be disposed of within this period of six months. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq has submitted that it is impossible for the civil suit to be disposed of within this period of six months. From the submission made by Mr. T.H. Khan, learned Counsel for the respondents, it appears that after the expiry of the period of six months extension of this period of stay would be necessary and that the trial Court would be competent to grant the extension. This means the civil suit may drag on for a long time. In view of this position, this appeal should be disposed of on merit. 

 4. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq has contended that when the criminal case on a definite allegation crones. of commission of offences was filed long before, it was highly improper for the High Court Division to stay the proceeding of the criminal case particularly when it was evident that disposal of the title suit would be impossible within such a short time. Learned counsel argues that disposal of a civil suit takes several years, whereas sound administration of criminal justice requires that justice should be done as quickly as possible either by punishing the accused if found guilty or acquitting him if found innocent. He, however, agrees that the Court may in its discretion stay proceedings of a criminal case pending disposal of a civil suit but this discretion, he contends, must be exercised for the ends of justice and not arbitrarily. The learned counsel has referred to the series of steps taken by the accused persons from the very beginning to obstruct the proceedings of the criminal case. Secondly, he has contended, the subject matters of the criminal case and that of the subsequently instituted civil suit are not exactly the same; he has pointed out that there is a specific allegation of defalcation of a huge amount of money by forging, or using forged documents such as cheques and vouchers and this allegation as to commission of criminal offence is by itself sufficient for continuation of the criminal proceeding without any interruption. Mr. T.H. Khan has contended that there is nothing in the record to show that the discretion has been arbitrarily or wrongly exercised by the High Court Division granting the stay. 

 5. The judgment of the High Court Division however shows that the learned Judges expressed doubt about the justification for staying the criminal proceeding for an indefinite period but granted the stay thinking that the civil suit might be disposed of within this period. This is , as we see, an impossibility. There is no hard and fast rule where the court's discretion staying the proceeding of a criminal case may be exercised. There is also no hard and fast rule that if the criminal proceeding is started earlier and the civil suit is instituted later no stay of the criminal proceeding shall be granted. We find the question of stay is one of judicial discretion of the Court having regard to the facts and circumstances of a given case. If the finding of the civil suit is likely to prejudice the accused then the question of stay should be given favourable consideration. In this case attempts were made by the respondents in many forums for stopping the course of criminal justice and having been unsuccessful they filed the suit. The principle governing the stay of proceedings of civil suit vis-a-vis Criminal cases is that the criminal matters should be given precedence. This question was considered by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of M.S. Sharif v. State of Madras, AIR 1964 SC 397. In that case, a criminal prosecution under section 193, for giving false evidence and a civil suit claiming damage for wrongful detention were started on the same facts. The Supreme Court refused stay of the criminal case and stayed the civil suit for swift disposal of the former and observed, among other things that the possibility of conflicting decision by civil and criminal courts is not a ground for stay of the criminal proceeding when law does not provide that the decision of the one is binding upon the other. 

 6. Having considered the nature of the allegation as appears from the complaint petition vis-a-vis the contention of the accused-- persons formulated in the plaint of their suit, we are of the view that the criminal case should be disposed of as quickly as possible so that justice may be available to the parties without unnecessary delay, that is, by conviction of the accused if guilty or by acquittal if they are not. We therefore hold that the impugned order of the High Court Division is not proper and justified.
